children: Layoffs, return-to-office battles and AI-led change have piled onto HR’s plate, prompting four CHROs to call for stronger support systems for the people managing them

Every HR Professionals Day, the conversation circles back to what HR does for everyone else — onboarding, layoffs, culture, employee wellbeing and the difficult conversations that come with organisational change. Far less often is the question asked: who does this for HR itself?

The question is becoming harder to ignore as the demands placed on HR continue to expand. A global study by SHRM found that HR professionals’ confidence in their organisation’s mental health support fell from 70 per cent in 2024 to 65 per cent in 2025. Meanwhile, a Deloitte study on workplace mental health found that more than half of employees surveyed across Indian industries reported emotional exhaustion and burnout — challenges HR teams are expected to identify and address, even as their own pressures receive less attention.

For HR leaders, the challenge is not simply managing a larger workload. It is the emotional and organisational responsibility of helping employees navigate uncertainty while often experiencing that uncertainty themselves.
The Load Has Intensified

For Megha Goel, Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO), Godrej Properties, the shift is less about entirely new problems and more about existing challenges arriving simultaneously, leaving little room to process one before the next begins."A high emotional quotient is no longer a nice to have for HR, it is treated as the baseline, with fairness, objectivity and empathy sitting at the heart of it," said Goel.

Layoffs in one part of a business while keeping the wider workforce engaged, return-to-office conversations that touch personal circumstances, and AI-led changes that raise questions about employees’ relevance have created what Goel describes as "a very different kind of labour, repeated across audiences, day after day."

The pressure also comes from HR’s role in shaping organisational culture. While culture is intended to be a shared leadership responsibility, HR often designs and facilitates it and is held accountable when it falters. The question of who supports the people carrying that responsibility, however, is less frequently addressed.
Leading Change Alone

Sonal Jain, Global Chief Human Resource and Transformation Officer, EPL, sees the challenge as structural rather than simply emotional. HR frequently finds itself at the centre of the same organisational changes it is expected to help employees navigate."I believe organisations need to build an ecosystem where people across functions are able to look after each other, with support systems, processes and people they can look up to," said Jain.

One additional challenge is confidentiality. HR professionals routinely handle sensitive information that cannot be discussed with colleagues or peers, making formal and confidential support mechanisms particularly important.

Jain pointed to mechanisms such as Employee Assistance Programmes and confidential feedback channels as potential avenues for HR professionals to seek support without compromising the confidentiality inherent to their roles.

For Pooja Singh, CHRO, PSPL Group, the isolation can also stem from how HR is perceived within an organisation. The function’s proximity to performance management, workplace concerns and organisational decisions can make its presence feel evaluative, making it harder to build the informal relationships that often help employees manage workplace pressure."A sustainable HR function is not one that simply absorbs pressure," said Singh. "It is one that has the authority, resources, support and organisational trust to manage complexity effectively."
Beyond Wellness Programmes

The four CHROs converge on a broader point: wellness programmes alone cannot address the pressures facing HR.For Goel, organisational credibility is central. When HR is trusted to lead through functional expertise and business context, it has greater room to handle difficult situations effectively. Leadership support is equally important, particularly when HR has to communicate or implement unpopular decisions.

Singh argues that responsibility for employee wellbeing and organisational culture cannot rest with HR alone."Managers and business leaders must share accountability for employee well-being, workplace culture and successful change," she said. "HR can provide the framework, expertise and leadership, but it cannot be the organisation's sole emotional and cultural shock absorber."

Jain believes HR also needs a stronger voice in decisions it is subsequently expected to execute, particularly when leaders are dealing with difficult organisational choices. She argues that this voice should be supported by data and analytics rather than instinct alone."Culture is built piece by piece, and if one part of that foundation is removed, the whole structure can be affected," she said.

For Shikha Gupta, CHRO, Luminous Power Technologies, one of the most practical gaps lies in how HR uses the wellbeing resources it makes available to others."It is important that we proactively leverage them for our own wellbeing and resilience," said Gupta.
Boundaries As A Skill

For Gupta, one of the most important lessons in sustaining an HR leadership role is understanding the relationship between empathy and boundaries."Empathy is most effective when paired with healthy boundaries," she said. "Sustaining yourself is not separate from being an effective leader; it is an essential part of it."

Singh similarly distinguishes resilience from simply absorbing organisational pressure. For HR professionals, resilience cannot mean carrying the weight of difficult decisions and employee concerns in isolation.

That distinction is increasingly relevant as the function’s remit expands. HR leaders are expected to support employees through restructuring, changing work models, technology-led transformation and evolving expectations around wellbeing, while also advising business leaders and protecting organisational culture.
Building Support For HR

Across the four conversations, the common thread is not a call for HR to step away from its responsibilities, but for organisations to recognise that the function itself needs an ecosystem of support.

That could mean greater leadership accountability for employee wellbeing, confidential support mechanisms for HR professionals, stronger peer networks, clearer boundaries and greater organisational backing when HR teams make difficult decisions.

For a function tasked with building resilient workplaces, the question is therefore increasingly reciprocal: what structures are organisations creating to ensure that the people supporting everyone else have the support, authority and space to sustain themselves?As Singh puts it, if HR’s job is to build resilient organisations, “it is equally important that HR is resilient enough to take the lead.”
